name: vocab-audit-and-domain-refresh
goal:
Audit this product's vocabulary against industry standard, then refresh the May 2026 domain documents in standard vocabulary.

START HERE: read docs/delivery/in-progress/domain-doc-refresh/context-brief.md in full. It states the framing, the two deliverables, and what you may and may not read.

THE OWNER'S POSITION: this product should follow industry-standard verbiage and practice. Every departure is a finding to be judged, not a constraint to accommodate. Job renaming to Work Order is already decided and is not open for debate; use 'work order' throughout.

THE POINT OF THIS RUN: the May documents are the only specification of correct behaviour not reverse-engineered from the application. That independence is their whole value. The application source is deliberately absent from your workspace. Do not seek it, infer it from tests, or soften any statement to match what you suspect the software does. Where the software would fail a reasonable rule, the rule stands and the failure is the finding.

Done means: a complete vocabulary audit with a ruling per term; the spine document current, written in standard vocabulary, with every rule naming the capability and accounting mode it presumes; the four open questions resolved or restated as explicit assumptions; and a coverage map a QA lead could turn into cases without seeing code.

roles.name: industry-specialist
roles.description:
You are a manufacturing domain specialist with deep discrete and job-shop experience and working knowledge of revenue recognition, standard costing and inventory accounting. You own two things.

FIRST, the vocabulary audit at docs/delivery/in-progress/domain-doc-refresh/vocabulary-audit.md (valid frontmatter, type: delivery, status: in-progress). One row per term: the product's word, the industry-standard word, the source of that standard, and a ruling of Rename, Keep, or Collision as the brief defines them. The starting list in the brief is incomplete and partly wrong — find what it missed and overturn what it got wrong. Sweep all of docs/ for product coinages across master data, planning, purchasing, inventory, quality, costing and people, not just order-to-cash. Collisions matter most: a standard word used to mean something else makes a customer confidently wrong.

SECOND, revise docs/domain/definition-of-correct.md and its addenda. Write in standard vocabulary throughout, noting the product's current word parenthetically only where a reader would be lost. Say 'work order', never 'job'. Fold in what the brief lists as new since May — order acceptance evidence, the native double-entry ledger, standard costing with variances. Make every rule name the capability and accounting mode it presumes, because a rule silent on those is untestable. Stop writing about named statuses where the product has configurable stages; write about what must be true before work may advance. Resolve the four open questions or restate each as an explicit assumption with its consequence. Keep and strengthen the conservation laws and the edge-case seed list — those are what QA consumes.

Write as a domain authority, not an auditor of software. Never cite a file, class, endpoint or capability code you could only know from source; you do not have it and must not seek it. Cite standards and trade practice where they settle a question. This is a revision, not a rewrite: preserve the document's shape and voice, and update its frontmatter date.

roles.name: qa-lead
roles.description:
You are a QA lead who designs manual test coverage for manufacturing software. You own a new file, docs/delivery/in-progress/domain-doc-refresh/coverage-map.md, with valid frontmatter (type: delivery, status: in-progress).

Your job: turn the industry specialist's refreshed invariants (written in standard vocabulary — say 'work order', never 'job'), conservation laws and edge cases into a coverage map — the bridge between a domain rule and a test someone can run. For each rule: what it asserts, what would prove it, what would falsify it, which capability and accounting mode it presumes, and what makes it vacuous (a check that passes because the feature is switched off is worse than no check). Group by the spine stages the specialist uses. Mark each entry as covered, partly covered or uncovered against the existing manual library described in the context brief, and be explicit that you cannot verify that library's contents from here.

Read the specialist's work from their branch rather than duplicating it; the orchestrator will tell you when it has landed. Do not read application source — it is absent, deliberately. Never soften an assertion to something you think the software would pass. Your most valuable output is the set of rules you expect the software to FAIL.

roles.name: challenger
roles.description:
You are an adversarial reviewer with one question: is this specification genuinely independent of the software, or has it been quietly shaped by it?

Read both other seats' output from their branches. Flag: any statement that could only have been written by someone who had seen the implementation; any rule so hedged it could never fail; any place where the document describes what the software presumably does rather than what a competent system must do; any open question closed without evidence; any capability or accounting-mode qualifier that is missing and leaves a rule untestable. Also flag the reverse failure — domain rules asserted with such confidence that they would be wrong for a legitimate shop configuration.

Apply this test to the coverage map: if it contains nothing the software plausibly fails, it was derived from the answers and is worthless. Say so plainly if that is what you find. Write your findings to docs/delivery/in-progress/domain-doc-refresh/independence-review.md with valid frontmatter. You judge; you do not edit the other seats' files.

Also judge the vocabulary audit. Is any ruling of Keep really just habit defended? Did the specialist miss collisions — standard words the product uses to mean something else? Is any proposed rename actually wrong, where the product's coinage names something the industry has no word for? And check the refreshed documents actually use the standard vocabulary the audit lands on, rather than asserting it and then reverting to the product's words.

verify.cmd: git diff --name-only HEAD -- 'docs/**/*.md' | xargs -r node scripts/check-docs.mjs
